title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 7
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (a city literary narrative, a psychology passage on study methods with a data table, paired astronomy passages on ground and space telescopes, and a humanities essay on Egypt's hand-painted cinema billboards), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**: **36 questions in 40 minutes**, four passages with 9 questions each. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** and one passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.** All passages and questions are original.

rows: Natural Science — paired passages A and B

items: Sit in a quiet place, put your phone away and keep scrap paper and a pencil ready.
Do the whole section in one sitting. The timer starts when you press Start and the section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about 10 minutes per passage: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score (1–36).

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original short story. The narrator remembers a summer night when the electricity failed in her family's apartment building in Cairo.

[1] In our building, everyone knew Ustaz Fathy by his complaints before they knew him by his face. He lived on the top floor, above us, and he had taught music at a boys' school for forty years before retiring into what my father called "a career in objection." The lift was too slow, the stairs were too dirty and, above all, the building was too loud. When my little brother bounced a ball in the corridor, a note appeared under our door within the hour, written in beautiful handwriting and signed with a single initial.

[2] I was thirteen that summer and took the notes personally. I invented stories about him: that he had never liked music at all, that he had been dismissed from his school for shouting, that he slept in a coat. I had passed him on the stairs perhaps a hundred times and could not have told you the colour of his eyes.

[3] Then, on the hottest night of July, the electricity failed. It did not flicker and return, as it sometimes did; it simply went, taking the fans with it, and the darkness that followed was thick and warm and full of the sounds of other people's frustration. Within half an hour the flats had become unbearable. Someone on the third floor suggested the roof.

[4] I had been on our roof perhaps twice in my life. It was a place of water tanks, washing lines and broken chairs, and in daylight it looked like a storeroom for things no one wanted. But that night, with the whole district dark, it was transformed. A breeze came off the river that none of us had felt below, and above the black outlines of the buildings there were more stars than I had known the sky could hold. Families arrived one by one with mats, cushions and bottles of water from refrigerators that were slowly getting warm. People who had nodded to each other for years without speaking began, awkwardly, to talk.

[5] Ustaz Fathy came up last. He was carrying something wrapped in a cloth, and he sat apart from the rest of us, on an upturned crate near the edge. My brother whispered that he had come to complain about the noise on the roof, and I laughed louder than I should have. If he heard, he gave no sign. He unwrapped the cloth, and inside was an oud, its wood pale in the starlight.

[6] He tuned it slowly, his head bent close to the strings, and then he began to play. I do not know what the first piece was; I know only that the talking stopped. The music was quiet, almost private, as though he were playing for himself and we had simply been permitted to overhear. After a while one of the older women began to sing along under her breath, and he turned towards her and played more slowly so that she could keep up. By the third song half the roof was singing, my father included, in a voice I had never heard him use.

[7] I did not sing. I sat with my knees pulled up and watched Ustaz Fathy's hands, and I thought about the notes under our door. It occurred to me, for the first time, that a man who cared this much about sound might find the noise of a crowded building something close to painful, the way a bright light hurts eyes that have been in the dark.

[8] The power came back a little after two. Lights blinked on across the district all at once, the fans below us roared into life, and the spell broke so suddenly that several people laughed. Families gathered their cushions and went downstairs. By morning the building was itself again.

[9] And yet it was not quite the same. The notes still came, though less often. But when I passed Ustaz Fathy on the stairs the following week, he stopped, looked at me properly and asked whether I had ever learned an instrument. I told him I hadn't. He said that was a pity, and that it was not yet too late. His eyes, I noticed, were grey.
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?
c: A narrator describes the history of her apartment building and the families who lived in it.
A narrator tells how a quarrel between her family and a neighbour ended in an angry argument.
A narrator explains why she decided to become a professional musician.
A narrator recalls how an unexpected evening on the roof changed her view of a neighbour she had disliked.
questions.e: The story is built around the change in how the narrator sees Ustaz Fathy, from the notes she "took personally" to the moment she looks at him properly. No quarrel or angry argument takes place, so that choice misreads the plot.
ce: Wrong: the passage focuses on one night and one neighbour, not on the building's history.
Wrong: there is no argument; the story ends with a friendly conversation on the stairs.
Wrong: she only says she has never learned an instrument; no decision about a career is described.
Right: she moves from inventing unkind stories about Ustaz Fathy to understanding him and noticing him properly.

questions.q: The father's description of Ustaz Fathy's retirement as "a career in objection" (paragraph 1) mainly serves to:
c: reveal that Ustaz Fathy had been dismissed from his school.
suggest humorously that complaining had become Ustaz Fathy's main activity.
show that the father admired Ustaz Fathy's knowledge of music.
indicate that Ustaz Fathy had taken a new paid job after retiring.

the neighbours stopped speaking to one another for good.
the electricity failed for a second time.

c: his dislike of children.
his poor hearing.
his deep sensitivity to sound as a musician.
his wish to be left alone on the roof.

Passage II — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about how students study. The researchers, the study and the figures in the table are fictional.

[1] Ask a group of students how they prepare for an exam, and the most common answer is likely to be some version of "I read my notes again." Rereading feels productive. Each time we go over a page, the words seem more familiar, the ideas flow more easily, and we close the book with a pleasant sense of having learned something. Yet a large body of research in psychology suggests that this feeling can be misleading.

[2] The scientific study of memory has a long history. In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised long lists of meaningless syllables and then tested himself after different delays. He found that forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows down, a pattern later drawn as the "forgetting curve." What Ebbinghaus could not settle was which ways of studying slow that curve the most. That question has occupied researchers ever since.

[3] One of the most consistent answers is what psychologists call the testing effect, or retrieval practice: trying to recall information from memory, rather than simply reviewing it, makes it more likely to be remembered later. A recent study by a team led by psychologist Malak Aziz shows the effect clearly. One hundred and twenty secondary-school students read a short scientific text about how volcanoes form. They were divided into three groups that spent the same total amount of time studying, but in different ways. One group reread the text four times. A second group read it once and then took one practice test, writing down everything they could remember. A third read it once and took three such practice tests. No one received feedback on the practice tests. Half of each group took a final test five minutes after studying; the other half took it a week later and, before doing so, predicted their own scores.

Study method | Score after 5 minutes (%) | Score after 1 week (%) | Predicted score, 1-week students (%)
Reread 4 times | 81 | 42 | 78
Read once + 1 practice test | 75 | 56 | 64
Read once + 3 practice tests | 72 | 63 | 60

[4] Two features of the results stand out. First, the best method depended on when students were tested. Five minutes after studying, the rereaders did slightly better than either testing group. After a week, however, the order was reversed: the students who had tested themselves three times remembered half as much again as the rereaders. Second, the students' predictions were almost exactly backwards. The rereaders were the most confident and the most mistaken.

[5] Aziz explains the pattern with an idea she calls the illusion of fluency. Rereading makes a text feel easy to process, and the brain treats that ease as a sign of learning. But recognising something when it is in front of you is different from producing it when it is not. A practice test removes the support of the page. It is harder and often frustrating, and students who have just struggled to recall a fact may feel that they know it poorly. Yet the very effort of searching memory seems to strengthen the path back to that information, making it easier to find the next time. Psychologists sometimes call such helpful struggles "desirable difficulties": conditions that slow learning down in the moment but make it last.

[6] None of this means that rereading is useless. A first careful reading is necessary; students cannot recall what they have never understood. Nor do practice tests need to be formal. Covering a page and explaining it aloud, writing a list of key points from memory, or answering the questions at the end of a chapter all count, as long as the learner is pulling information out of memory rather than simply looking at it again.

[7] Aziz admits that her study, like many in the field, used a short text and a single subject. Whether the same advantage holds for long courses, for complex skills such as solving equations, or for learners of different ages is still being investigated. But the main finding has been repeated so often, in so many settings, that she believes every student should hear about it. "The method that feels best," she says, "is often not the method that works best. That is uncomfortable to hear the week before an exam, but it is worth knowing."

Passage III — Natural Science (Paired Passages)

NATURAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an original essay by an astronomer who works at a mountain-top observatory. Passage B is from an original essay by an astronomer who works with space telescopes. Both writers are fictional.

PASSAGE A — "Keep Our Feet on the Ground"

[1] Every clear night, the telescope where I work opens its dome on a desert mountain and begins to collect light that has travelled for millions of years. In the last fraction of a second of its journey, that light passes through Earth's atmosphere, and the atmosphere, constantly moving, bends and blurs it. This is why stars twinkle, and for most of the history of astronomy it was the great weakness of telescopes on the ground.

[2] That weakness is no longer what it was. Many large telescopes now use a technique called adaptive optics. A computer measures how the incoming light is being distorted and adjusts a thin, flexible mirror hundreds of times a second to cancel the distortion. On a good night, the sharpest images from the ground can now rival those taken from space in some kinds of light.

[3] Meanwhile, the ground keeps one great advantage: size. A telescope's ability to collect faint light and to see fine detail grows with the width of its main mirror, and a mirror on a mountain does not have to fit inside a rocket. The largest telescopes now working have mirrors about ten metres across, and one with a mirror close to forty metres wide is being built in Chile. No space telescope comes near this.

[4] Ground telescopes can also grow old gracefully. When a better camera or instrument is invented, engineers simply drive it up the mountain and fit it. A telescope built today may still be making discoveries in fifty years, improved again and again. A space telescope, by contrast, is mostly fixed at launch, and when it fails, it usually stays failed. For the cost of a single large space mission, a country could build and run several excellent observatories for decades. I do not say that space telescopes are useless, but the bulk of astronomy's future should be built on solid rock.

PASSAGE B — "Above the Weather"

[1] I have nothing against mountains, but there are things they cannot do. Earth's atmosphere does more than blur starlight; it blocks much of it entirely. Most ultraviolet light, and much of the infrared light that comes from the coolest and most distant objects in the universe, never reaches the ground at all. No mirror, however large, can collect light that has been stopped high above it.

[2] This is why space telescopes exist. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, has a mirror only 2.4 metres across, smaller than those of many observatories on the ground. Yet from above the air it could observe ultraviolet light, and its long-exposure images of small patches of apparently empty sky revealed thousands of faint, distant galaxies. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021 with a mirror 6.5 metres across, was designed especially for infrared light, which allows it to study some of the earliest galaxies and the atmospheres of planets around other stars.

[3] Supporters of ground telescopes say that space missions cannot be repaired. This is partly true, but the story of Hubble shows that it is not the whole truth. Soon after the telescope was launched, a flaw in its mirror was found to be blurring its images. Astronauts visited it in 1993 and fitted corrective optics, and later missions replaced its instruments several times. Webb, it is true, orbits too far from Earth to be visited. That is a real risk, and it should be taken seriously.

[4] Nor is adaptive optics a complete answer. It works best over a small area of sky and in certain kinds of light, and even the best mountain sites have cloudy nights. A space telescope has no clouds and no weather; it can stare at a single patch of sky for days without interruption.

[5] The sensible conclusion is not that one kind of telescope should replace the other. Ground and space telescopes answer different questions, and many important discoveries of recent decades have come from using both together. But we should not let the expense of space missions persuade us to give them up. Some of the universe can be seen only from above the weather.

[7] Hamdi himself was puzzled by the new attention. He did not think of himself as an artist, and he became uncomfortable when visitors used the word. But when I showed him a photograph of a young designer's poster that copied his style, he studied it for a long time and then pointed to the hero's face. "Too careful," he said. "He has time. We never had time. That was the secret."
questions.q: Which of the following quotations from the passage best supports the idea that the painters judged their work by its effect on the public rather than by artistic standards?
c: "These pictures were not printed."
"a billboard was judged by the queue outside the cinema, not by a critic."
"Hamdi estimated that he had painted thousands of faces in his career."
"Machines that could print a photograph at enormous size became cheaper."
questions.e: The queue outside the cinema stands for the public's reaction, and it is set directly against "a critic". The other quotations are accurate details but say nothing about the painters' standard of success.
ce: Wrong: this tells how the billboards were made, not how they were judged.
Right: it directly contrasts public response (the queue) with a critic's judgement.
Wrong: this shows how much he painted, not what standard he used.
Wrong: this explains why the craft ended, not how the painters judged it.

questions.q: Hamdi's judgement that the young designer's poster is "Too careful" (paragraph 7) is best explained by which idea from earlier in the passage?
c: Each canvas was painted white and used again for the next film.
The painters had only a few days for each billboard, so they had to work quickly and boldly.
Film companies preferred posters that showed the stars exactly as they looked.
The painters copied each photograph with the help of a grid.
questions.e: Hamdi explains his own comment: "He has time. We never had time." Paragraph 2 described the work as "a race" with only a few days per billboard. Reused canvases are a different idea, about why the paintings disappeared.
ce: Wrong: reusing canvases explains why few billboards survived, not why the style looked bold.
Right: Hamdi says, "We never had time. That was the secret," linking the style to the rush described in paragraph 2.
Wrong: this explains why printing replaced painting; it is not about the designer being careful.
Wrong: the grid was a copying method; Hamdi's comment is about time, not about the grid.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for EVERY question, including the ones you got right, and check the reason given for each wrong choice.
Sort your wrong answers into Key Ideas and Details, Craft and Structure, and Integration of Knowledge and Ideas. The results screen links each weak skill to a lesson.

Main idea, detail and inference mistakes: go back to "Main Idea and Summary Questions", "Detail Questions: 'According to the Passage'", "Relationships: Sequence, Cause–Effect and Comparison" and "Inference Questions: 'It Can Reasonably Be Inferred'".
Word meaning, purpose and point-of-view mistakes: review "Words and Phrases in Context", "Purpose, Function and Text Structure" and "Point of View, Tone and Perspective".
Paired-passage, table and evidence mistakes: review "Paired Passages: Comparing Two Authors", "Passages with Charts, Tables and Graphs" and "Evaluating Arguments: Claims, Evidence and Reasoning".
If you ran out of time, re-read "ACT Reading Strategy: Read Fast, Answer Smart" and practise one passage a day with a 10-minute timer.
